column4: The next ayah identifies the transgressors as the destination for whom Hell waits; it completes 78:21's مِرْصَادًا without making the watchpoint morally indiscriminate.
Even if the deniers saw a piece of the sky falling, they would call it a piled cloud; their eye misreads an overhead blow as ordinary weather just as ʿĀd misread the approaching cloud.
Destroyed generations stronger in force ranged through the lands but found no escape, an unusually close meeting of country-crossers, the waiting judgment, and the limit no traveler can pass.
People are told to walk through the earth's paths and eat God's provision, yet resurrection is to Him; route, measured livelihood, and unavoidable destination share one ayah.
The one who worships on an edge is content when good comes but turns away under a trial, enacting the section's division of one divine testing into two opposite verdicts.
When people taste mercy after adversity they plot against the signs, while God's messengers record their plotting; changed provision, bad inward reading, and unseen observers coincide.
A secure town with abundant provision becomes ungrateful and is made to taste encompassing hunger and fear, directly overturning abundance as proof of lasting honor.
Many towns exulting in their livelihood are destroyed and left as scarcely inhabited dwellings, making prosperity's false reading visible in ruins to later observers.
Disbelievers must not read divine respite as good for themselves; the delay only lets sin increase before humiliating punishment, matching the watcher who waits rather than chases.
Those denying the signs are led gradually toward destruction from where they do not know, a direct statement of the hidden watch disclosed only at the blow.
God grants the deniers respite because His plan is firm, completing 7:182's unnoticed approach to capture.
God tells the messenger to leave the denier to Him, for He will lead such people gradually from where they do not know; the stationary watcher governs the approach.
The respite granted after 68:44 rests on a firm plan, distinguishing delayed seizure from absence of observation.
The opponents devise a plot, setting up the human attempt to control where and when another will be caught.
God answers their plot with His own plan, disclosing the true watcher behind the apparent ambush of 86:15.
The command to grant the disbelievers a little respite makes waiting part of the divine counter-plan rather than evidence that they escaped it.
Punishment has an appointed time and will come suddenly while its subjects do not perceive, closely matching travelers learning of the watcher only when struck.
While they demand punishment be hastened, Hell already encompasses the disbelievers; this supplies the unseen surrounding reality behind 29:53's sudden arrival.
On that day the human asks where escape lies, posing the road-traveler's question only after the hidden checkpoint has become visible.
The answer says there is no refuge, closing every alternate route raised by 75:10.
The final destination that day is to the Lord, completing the no-escape sequence with the place every traveler reaches.
Criminals are recognized by their marks and seized by forelocks and feet, so the watcher needs neither pursuit nor testimony to distinguish those arriving.
The question asks whether people see what surrounds them of sky and earth before warning of earth swallowing or fragments falling from above; sight, enclosure, and the blow meet directly.
People are asked whether they reflect within themselves before 30:9 asks them to travel and see former peoples' end, explicitly pairing inward and outward observation.
When criminals see the angels they receive no good news and cry حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا; seeing and the source's h-j-r boundary-word coincide at judgment.
Favor makes the human turn away in self-importance, while evil makes him despair, a concise statement of the same two mistaken reactions to one Lord's testing.
People rejoice when made to taste mercy and immediately despair when harm from their own deeds reaches them, repeating the divided reading of opposed conditions.
A human rejoices at mercy but becomes ungrateful when calamity follows his deeds, another exact contrast in inward responses to changing provision.
The human being is created anxiously grasping, introducing the unstable inward disposition behind the section's two judgments.
When evil touches him he becomes impatient, specifying the deprivation-side response of the human described in 70:19.
When good touches him he withholds it, completing the paired response and showing that abundance itself exposes rather than certifies him.
When mercy is removed after being tasted, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful, explicitly treating deprivation as a final verdict.
When blessing follows hardship, the human boasts that his troubles are gone, mirroring the opposite error about renewed abundance.
Affliction makes a person call on God in every posture, but relief makes him pass on as though he never called, showing self-perception changing with circumstance.
The person who is stingy and sees himself self-sufficient repeats the very inward estimate stated in 96:7.
He denies the finest truth, identifying the moral judgment joined to self-sufficiency in 92:8.
He is eased toward hardship, a pointed reversal of the ease his wealth seemed to promise.
His wealth will not avail him when he falls, making the final blow expose the false self-estimate of 92:8.
The faulted person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, fixing his gaze on the very abundance by which he measures himself.
He thinks his wealth makes him immortal, the most extreme form of reading provision as personal security.
He will instead be hurled into the Crusher, the sudden destination that overturns the inward verdict in 104:3.
A person whose evil deed is beautified so that he sees it as good gives a direct Quranic case of the inward eye manufacturing a false judgment.

God attacks plotters' building from its foundations so the roof falls on them from above and punishment comes from where they do not perceive, closely reproducing the hidden watcher and overhead pounce.
Those plotting evil are asked whether they feel secure from being swallowed by earth or seized from where they do not perceive.
God may seize them during their movement about, and they cannot frustrate Him; the travelers' motion does not evade the waiting judgment of 16:45.
People are asked whether they feel secure from an encompassing punishment or the Hour arriving suddenly while unaware, directly naming the unperceived encounter.
The disbelievers' free movement through the lands must not deceive the observer, warning against reading unhindered travel as escape from the watcher.
That movement is only brief enjoyment before Hell becomes their resting-place, completing 3:196's correction.
The disbelievers' movement through the lands must not deceive the addressee, repeating the warning that apparent freedom on the route is temporary.
Pharaoh and the overturned towns come with wrongdoing, continuing the observed catalogue from Thamūd and ʿĀd to the third ruler named by the section.
They disobey their Lord's messenger, so He seizes them with an overwhelming seizure; this supplies the blow joining the peoples listed in 69:5-9.
The sending of the barren wind against ʿĀd gives another direct scene of the Lord's action that the observer of 89:6 is asked to see.
The wind leaves everything it passes like ruins, supplying the visible aftermath of 51:41's divine act.
Thamūd are granted enjoyment for a time before the thunderbolt of 51:44, making respite precede the blow in the same passage.
A furious wind is sent against ʿĀd over ill-fated days so they taste disgrace, standing between their self-estimate in 41:15 and Thamūd's blinded choice in 41:17.
God has destroyed towns around the audience and varied the signs so people might return, turning ʿĀd's sensory failure in 46:24-26 into a road-side warning for later observers.
The believers ask God to pour patience upon them, using ص ب ب for sustaining firmness before battle rather than for a scourge poured upon transgressors.
Pharaoh's threatened believers ask their Lord to pour patience upon them, reversing the source's punitive pour while retaining descent from the true sovereign above Pharaoh.
Those who remain patient and do good are excepted from the despair and boasting in 11:9-10, marking the right response across both conditions.
The wicked are veiled from their Lord on that day, a boundary on human sight that does not limit the divine watcher who has seen them throughout.
The addressees are asked whether they feel secure from the One above causing the earth to swallow them, one half of the above-and-below enclosure completed by 67:17.
Wealth and children must not inspire admiration, because they can themselves belong to worldly punishment rather than signal divine favor.
Wealth and children are explicitly a trial, directly denying their use as a simple measure of honor.
Possessions and children are again named as a test, while the great reward remains with God rather than in the visible abundance.
The Prophet is told not to stretch his eyes toward worldly splendor given to groups as a test, and that his Lord's provision is better and more lasting.
Fear, hunger, and loss are announced as forms of testing, giving deprivation an explicit purpose other than humiliation.
The garden-owner measures himself as greater in wealth and followers, beginning a self-image constructed from visible abundance.
He enters his garden while wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, turning prosperity into imagined permanent security.
He doubts the Hour and expects an even better return if brought to his Lord, extending the false wealth-to-honor inference into the Hereafter.
His produce is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, the visible collapse that corrects his judgments in 18:34-36.
The garden owners are explicitly tested, linking an apparently secure abundance to the trial its possessors fail to recognize.
They swear to harvest in the morning without making exception, displaying confidence in possession immediately before the unseen visitation.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while they sleep, a night-time watch and blow unknown to its owners.
The garden becomes dark and stripped by morning, making the hidden visitation of 68:19 visible only in its result.
The human is himself a witness to his ingratitude, supporting the section's inward image of the person looking upon his own condition.
His intense love of wealth names the attachment that distorts the self-witness in 100:7.
A person who takes desire as god has hearing and heart sealed and a covering placed over sight, depicting inward appetite disabling the eye's lesson.
One driven cloud yields rain and hail that God strikes or averts, while its lightning nearly takes sight; provision, selective overhead blow, and the vulnerable eye occupy one scene.
The night journey of God's servant from the Sacred Mosque to the farthest mosque is the Quran's signal occurrence of the source's س ر ي night-travel sense.
Signs in the earth are offered to the certain before 51:21 turns the observing gaze into people's own selves.
Every soul is commanded to look at what it has sent forward for tomorrow while God remains aware of its deeds, joining self-inspection to the divine watcher.
The person is told to read his own record and is sufficient as a reckoner against himself, a judgment-day form of inward self-observation.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what was earned, revealing that the traveler's own body has preserved the watch.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify to what their owners did, turning familiar bodily instruments into ready witnesses.
God has enumerated deeds that people forgot and is witness over everything, explaining how the patient watcher can disclose a complete record.
The book speaks truth against people because their actions were being transcribed, presenting the stored result of continuous observation.
The placed record omits neither small nor great deed, and wrongdoers find what they did present before them, the exhaustive evidence gathered by the watchers.
The People of al-Ḥijr deny the messengers, naming the historical community behind the rock-cutting Thamūd scene while also sounding the source's h-j-r word.
God gives the People of al-Ḥijr signs but they turn away, clarifying the failure of perception before their secure dwellings and seizure in 15:82-83.
At a person's death God is nearer than the gathered human observers, but they do not see; the unseen divine presence lies inside the visible watching scene.
God takes people by night, knows what they earn by day, and raises them until an appointed term before their return and accounting; night, observation, delay, and destination meet.
God creates the human from a mixed drop to test him and makes him hearing and seeing, joining trial to the very faculties by which it should be read.
God may take wrongdoers gradually amid fear, extending 16:45-46's sudden and movement-time seizures with a slower form of the same inescapable watch.
The One who owns heaven and earth is witness over everything, grounding the observing stance behind the severe seizure later named in 85:12.
The Lord's grip is severe, giving the decisive blow that completes the universal witnessing of 85:9.
The keys of the unseen belong to God, who knows every falling leaf and hidden grain, expressing a watch from which neither movement nor concealed place escapes.
Not even an atom in heaven or earth escapes the Lord, and all is in a clear record; hidden movement and recorded observation are joined.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making deeds themselves the final object shown to the observed person.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, completing the exact and morally differentiated disclosure at judgment.
God delays people to an appointed term rather than seizing them immediately for wrongdoing, another explicit account of the watcher waiting until the fixed point.
God delays creatures to an appointed term instead of taking them at once for what they earn; when the term comes, He has always been seeing His servants.
God spares none of Thamūd, continuing the destruction of ʿĀd in 53:50 before 53:52 diagnoses Noah's people as still more transgressive.
